events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11399v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) present significant challenges to source tracing of generated code, as LLM rewriting can substantially alter the syntactic and structural characteristics of watermarked code. However, existing watermarking methods often suffer severe performance degradation under LLM-based functionality-preserving rewriting attacks. We attribute this vulnerability not merely to the intensity of rewriting, but to a fundamental distribution mismatch between the perturbations encountered during watermark training and the global, non-deterministic rewriting behaviors induced by LLMs. In order to deal with this challenge, we propose RoCoMark, a Robust Code waterMarking framework that explicitly learns and adapts to LLM rewriting behaviors. RoCoMark is a multi-round minimax game between the watermark embedder and LLM rewriter. In each round, the embedder first learns threat profiling from LLM-rewritten code by optimizing the watermark encoder through contrastive learning and knowledge distillation while mitigating catastrophic representation drift. Then the embedder improves strategies by optimizing the watermark encoder and extractor simultaneously. Finally, an adaptive attack-evolution mechanism based on Reflexion and short- and long-term memory pools is applied, enabling continuous interaction between the watermark embedder and evolving rewriting strategies. This iterative attacker-defender process progressively improves the robustness of the watermark against diverse and previously unseen LLM rewriting behaviors.
events.title: RoCoMark: Robust Code Watermarking Against LLM-Based Functionality-Preserving Rewriting Attacks

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10595v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The limited computational resources of Internet of Things (IoT) devices present challenges for secure image processing. This paper presents a distributed chaotic image encryption system using independent Wi-Fi-connected ESP32-S3 microcontrollers. A master-worker architecture distributes image blocks through master-coordinated chaotic sequence management, maintaining one logically continuous chaotic sequence by assigning block-specific starting states independently of worker assignments. The implemented system uses reversible chaotic substitution (SUBSTITUTE), while Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)-signed discovery messages and Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 with mutual authentication secure device communication. Experimental evaluation using one, two, and four workers demonstrates a reduction in execution time from 43.215 to 15.878 seconds, achieving a speed-up of 2.72 times. The encrypted image achieves a Shannon entropy of 7.999940 bits/byte and near-zero adjacent-pixel correlation. Exact image recovery is verified through matching Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) hashes and a Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) value of 1.0. Additional experiments demonstrate successful encryption and decryption using different worker counts and block sizes, automatic task reassignment following worker failure, and rejection of a mismatched private key during TLS authentication. events.title: Design and Evaluation of Secure Distributed Chaotic Image Encryption on ESP32-S3

events.excerpt: arXiv:2509.16915v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we study differentially private mechanisms for functions whose outputs lie in a Euclidean Jordan algebra. Euclidean Jordan algebras capture many important mathematical structures and form the foundation of linear programming, second-order cone programming, and semidefinite programming. Our main contribution is a generic Gaussian mechanism for such functions, with sensitivity measured in $\ell_2$, $\ell_1$, and $\ell_\infty$ norms. Notably, this framework includes the important case where the function outputs are symmetric matrices, and sensitivity is measured in the Frobenius, nuclear, or spectral norm. We further derive private algorithms for solving symmetric cone programs under various settings, using a combination of the multiplicative weights update method and our generic Gaussian mechanism. As an application, we present differentially private algorithms for semidefinite programming, resolving a major open question posed by [Hsu, Roth, Roughgarden, and Ullman, ICALP 2014].
events.title: Differential Privacy for Euclidean Jordan Algebra with Applications to Private Symmetric Cone Programming

events.excerpt: We recommend that all atlantic-2 validators and node operators update to v6.8.0-rc3 . The update is required for RPC nodes. There is no governance proposal and no coordinated chain halt. v6.8.0-rc3 is a release candidate on top of v6.8.0-rc2 . It makes wide eth_getLogs queries cheaper for RPC nodes and stops them early when the client cancels ( #4744 , #4790 , #4791 , #4799 , #4802 ). It also includes the v6.7.4 trace fix, so debug_trace* loads a past block's full validator set ( #4811 ). Wide log queries (over 100 blocks) share a node-wide limit of 30 queries per second. You can now change it with large_log_query_rps under [evm] in app.toml . Set it to 0 to turn the limit off. If the key is missing, the limit stays at 30 ( #4800 ). How to Update Build v6.8.0-rc3 with git fetch --tags && git checkout v6.8.0-rc3 && make install . Stop the node. Replace the seid binary with v6.8.0-rc3 . If you use Cosmovisor, replace the binary in upgrades/v6.8/bin/ . Start the node. Make sure that seid version shows v6.8.0-rc3 and that the node syncs new blocks. What's Changed Backport release/v6.8 : Skip consensus params on eth_getLogs contexts by @seidroid [bot] in #4744 Backport release/v6.8 : Cache completed upgrades for RPC closest-upgrade lookups by @seidroid [bot] in #4789 Backport release/v6.8 : Read the last block height without hashing the commit info by @seidroid [bot] in #4788 Backport release/v6.8 : Read eth_getLogs watermarks once per range instead of per block by @seidroid [bot] in #4790 Backport release/v6.8 : Skip encoding Tendermint responses when tracing is off by @seidroi

events.excerpt: Posting a factual decode of recent ACLManager role activity on Aave V3 Ethereum, in the dated-report style already used in this category. Three RISK_ADMIN_ROLE grants since 2 September 2026: 2 Sep 2026, block 25891729 — granted to 0xbe28…7744 and 0x529e…F6c5 (two grants, same transaction) 30 Sep 2026, block 26089561 — granted to 0x6f48d9cdb8ee6e17c96b2d8aec128af426a295c1 The 30 Sep recipient is a verified contract named RiskSteward, 20,061 bytes of deployed code. All three grants were sent by 0x5300A1a15135EA4dc7aD5a167152C01EFc9b192A, which is the governance Executor. So these passed governance rather than originating from a standalone admin key — worth stating explicitly, since a RISK_ADMIN grant from an EOA would read very differently. Practical scope: RISK_ADMIN can change supply and borrow caps, LTVs, liquidation thresholds and reserve configuration without a full governance vote. Routing it through a RiskSteward contract constrains what the holder may change, which is the safer pattern, but each grant still widens the set of actors who can move risk parameters between votes. Context: the ARFC “Activate Aave Risk Stewards on Aave V4” thread is now closed with AIP #523 executed, so I’m posting this separately rather than reverting that thread. Method note: this is decoded from ACLManager’s RoleGranted logs plus the role constants read off the contract itself. I have not diffed storage layouts or reviewed the RiskSteward contract’s internal constraints — so I’m not making any claim about what that specific steward is or isn’t able to do.
